chunk_findings.detail: The merged order is the only snapshot-derived datum that is trusted without re-hashing. `_load_snapshot` sets `_SNAP_ORDER[dir]` as soon as the snapshot file is internally self-consistent, regardless of whether the current log bytes still match. Concrete input: a snapshot describing `a.log` with `consumed = N` and order `names/idxs`; then rewrite/compact/truncate `a.log` so that `sha256(data[:N]) != stored digest` (the snapshot file itself is left intact and still passes every header/payload check). On the next cold read, `_load_snapshot` sets `_SNAP_ORDER[dir]` from the stale snapshot, then `_seed_from_snapshot(a.log, data)` computes the prefix hash, finds it differs, and returns `None`, so `a.log` is fully re-parsed into a possibly different event list. `_SNAP_ORDER[dir]` is never cleared on that rejection, so any code path that consults it to skip the sort (the whole point of storing it) now applies indices that were computed for the snapshot's event list to the freshly parsed list — producing a different order than the full-parse path, or an IndexError if the re-parsed list is shorter. The intent's requirement that a stale snapshot be fully ignored is not met for the order; the fix is to tie the cached order to the same hash verification (e.g., only publish `_SNAP_ORDER` once every referenced shard has been seed-verified, or invalidate it whenever any referenced shard falls back to a full parse).

chunk_findings.detail:
The saved order is validated only for range (`min < 0` / `max >= len(base)`); it is never checked for duplicate indices, and an empty `order` skips validation entirely. A structurally valid but semantically wrong order array is therefore trusted, which is exactly the "corrupt snapshot must be ignored" case. The per-shard sha256 anchors the shard bytes to the snapshot's prefix, but nothing anchors the dir‑level `order` values, so a well‑formed-but-corrupted order (e.g. a single int bit‑flip from `[0,1,2,3]` to `[0,1,2,2]`, which passes `max < 4`) is adopted verbatim.

Concrete input: one live shard `s` whose complete prefix is `[E]`, with a dir snapshot `names=[("s",1)]`, `order=[0,0]`. The seeding checks pass (`d.parsed.seeded` is true, `snap_n == 1`), bounds pass (`max=0 < len(base)=1`), so `uniq = [base[0], base[0]] = [E, E]` and `read_all(snapshot=True)` returns `[E, E]`, while the full-parse path (`read_all(snapshot=False)`) returns `[E]`. The same happens with `names=[("s",1)]`, `order=[]` plus a non-empty `base` (order `[]` is falsy, so the bounds guard is skipped and every prefix event is silently dropped), and with a reordered/`max`-in-range permutation. In all cases the returned event list differs from the full-parse path, and because `_MERGED[self.dir]` is populated from this result, the wrong `uniq` is then served from cache to subsequent normal reads. Rejecting any `order` that is not a set of distinct in-range indices (i.e. `len(set(order)) != len(order)`, and an explicit empty-vs-non-empty-base check) would close this.

chunk_findings.detail: `_check` verifies only event *ids* (plus `skipped_lines`) and the callers additionally assert only parse counts — nothing in this file ever compares the event bodies (`data`, `ts`, `kind`, …) returned by the snapshot path against the full-parse path, even though the module docstring promises "the result must be byte-for-byte what the unoptimised path returns". That an id does *not* encode the rest of the payload is demonstrated by this very file: `test_verify_never_uses_the_snapshot` rewrites `forged[2] = {"title": "forged", "kind": "task"}` and recomputes only `meta["size"]`/`meta["sha256"]`, and `read_all()` happily loads the poisoned event (the test asserts the title "forged" is present). So a snapshot whose serializer keeps each event's id but drops/zeroes another field (e.g. `ts`) or swaps two events' payloads while preserving their ids yields exactly the same id sequence and the same `log.parsed` count. Concretely: hand-edit the payload the way the verify test does, but instead of changing a title, mutate a timestamp field for shard `b` only (recompute `size`/`sha256`), then run e.g. `test_a_cold_read_from_the_snapshot_parses_nothing_and_matches` (`parsed == 0`, ids unchanged) or `test_a_shard_changed_in_place_is_reparsed_the_others_are_not` (`parsed == N`, b served from the snapshot) — all pass, while the cold-read output differs from the full-parse output. Fixing this requires comparing the full event contents (or the serialized representation) in `_check`, not just `e.id`.

chunk_findings.detail:
The merged order is persisted and loaded as a single global blob (`body["\0order"] = (names, [where[id(e)] for e in merged.uniq])` at write time, `_SNAP_ORDER[self.dir] = (list(names), list(idxs))` at load time) that is validated only by the *file-level* sha256 in the header. Its indices are positions in the concatenation `[e for _, d in deltas for e in d.whole]`, i.e. they are only meaningful while every shard named in `names` still contains exactly the snapshotted event list. But `_seed_from_snapshot` can reject an individual shard on its per-shard prefix digest (`if h.hexdigest() != digest: return None`) *after* `_load_snapshot` has already installed `_SNAP_ORDER`, and nothing in this hunk removes or invalidates the order when a shard is rejected. The docstring's safety claim ("`_seed_from_snapshot` re-hashes the real bytes before using any of it") therefore holds for the per-shard `tuples`, but not for the order: the order is trusted wholesale on the basis of the file hash, not the shard bytes.

Concrete failure: snapshot is written for shards A and B, recording `names = [("A", n_A), ("B", n_B)]` and indices computed over A's events followed by B's events. Later B is rewritten (different events and/or a different count) while A is untouched. On the next cold read, A's digest matches and `_seed_from_snapshot` returns A's events, but B's digest fails, so B is fully re-parsed and its event list no longer matches the snapshotted B. If the caller applies `_SNAP_ORDER` (which the write-side comment "so a cold read can skip the sort" shows is the intent), the stored indices now select the wrong events from the new A+B concatenation — or raise `IndexError` when a stored index exceeds the new list length — producing output different from the full-parse path. The same happens if *every* shard's digest fails (all shards re-parsed, no seeds) yet `_SNAP_ORDER` remains set from the load.

The order needs to be tagged/validated per shard (or discarded unless every shard named

chunk_findings.detail: The saved `order` is only sanity-checked with `min(order) < 0 or max(order) >= len(base)`, and that check is skipped entirely when `order` is empty (`if order and (...)`). It is never verified that `order` is a permutation of `range(len(base))`. So a snapshot whose order is a strict subset (or a multiset with repeats) of the indices is accepted: `uniq = [base[i] for i in order]` then contains fewer (or duplicated) events than `base`. Concretely, take a snapshot that lists `names = [("a", 3)]` but has `order = []` (or `order = [0]`) — a truncated/edited-but-still-parseable snapshot file, exactly the "corrupt" case the change promises to ignore. The bound check passes (empty order, or `0` within `0..2`), so `_merged_from_snapshot` returns `_Merged({a: (gen, 3)}, [], set())`. Because `marks[a] = (gen, 3)` records that all three events of shard `a` were already consumed, `_merge` folds in only events appended beyond the seeded prefix and never re-adds the dropped ones, so `read_all()` returns fewer events than the full-parse path (or duplicate events when `order` repeats an index). The sha256 guard only covers the shard bytes, not the order encoding, so it cannot catch this; and by contrast the full-parse path (and `verify()`, thanks to `snapshot=False`) returns the correct set. The order must be rejected unless it is a permutation of `range(len(base))`.
